items.objective_statement: determine the gradient of the straight line graph
items.stem: To find the gradient of a straight line graph, a student should use

options.text: the two plotted points closest together

misconception.label: Close points give small differences, so the reading uncertainty matters far more.

options.text: a large triangle drawn on the line

misconception.label: The line need not pass through the origin, so using it can give the wrong gradient.

options.text: the first and last plotted points

misconception.label: Plotted points may lie slightly off the line; the triangle should be drawn on the line itself.

steps: The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x.
Every coordinate read from the graph carries a small uncertainty.
Using a large triangle makes those changes large, so the same uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of each, and the gradient is more accurate.
solution.answer_line: a large triangle drawn on the line

misconception.label: One significant figure throws away precision that was actually measured.

So the answer is rounded to three significant figures: 2.41 s.

items.objective_statement: determine the location of the centre of gravity of a body
items.stem: The centre of gravity of a uniform ring lies

misconception.label: Symmetry puts it at the middle, not on the rim.

options.text: at the centre of the hole
at the thickest part of the ring

misconception.label: A uniform ring has the same thickness all the way round.
It lies at the centre of the hole, which is inside the outline of the ring.

steps: A uniform ring is symmetrical about its centre.
Every small piece of the rim is balanced by the piece directly opposite it.
So the combined weight acts through the middle, and the centre of gravity of a body need not lie in the material of the body at all.
solution.answer_line: at the centre of the hole

items.objective_statement: relate the stability of an object to the position of its centre of gravity and its weight
items.stem: A cone resting on its point is in

misconception.label: In stable equilibrium a small push raises the centre of gravity and the body returns.
In neutral equilibrium the centre of gravity stays at the same height, as for a ball on a table.
It does balance, if placed exactly right, so it is in equilibrium.

steps: Balanced on its point, the cone's centre of gravity is as high as it can be.
Any small tilt lowers it.
The weight then acts outside the point of support and topples the cone further, so the equilibrium is unstable.
solution.answer_line: unstable equilibrium

items.stem: A bus carrying passengers only on the upper deck is less stable than one carrying them on the lower deck because the loaded bus has a

misconception.label: The mass is the same wherever the passengers sit.
Loading the upper deck raises the centre of gravity, it does not lower it.
The base is fixed by the width of the wheels and does not change.

steps: A vehicle topples when its centre of gravity passes outside the line of its wheels.
Passengers on the upper deck raise the centre of gravity.
A higher centre of gravity passes outside the wheelbase at a smaller tilt, so the bus overturns more easily.

items.stem: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of

misconception.label: The direction of motion is given by the velocity, not the acceleration.

items.stem: Which is an example of friction being useful rather than a nuisance?

misconception.label: Wear is one of the costs of friction.

options.text: The grip of a shoe on the ground

misconception.label: Heating in an engine is wasted energy.
Energy wasted in a bearing is exactly the nuisance friction causes.

steps: Friction resists sliding between surfaces in contact.
Pushing back on the ground with the foot works only because friction stops the foot sliding.
The same effect makes brakes and car tyres work, while wear and unwanted heating are the costs.
solution.answer_line: The grip of a shoe on the ground

misconception.label: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion; the stored water is still.

items.objective_statement: apply the law of conservation of energy
items.stem: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy

options.text: cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another
is always conserved as useful energy

misconception.label: Some of it always ends up as unusable thermal energy, which is why no machine is 100 per cent efficient.

options.text: is used up when work is done

misconception.label: Energy is transferred when work is done, not destroyed.

options.text: is created whenever a machine is switched on

misconception.label: No machine creates energy; it converts what it is supplied with.

steps: Follow the energy through any process and add up every form at the end.
The total is always the same as at the start.
What changes is the form, and usually some of it ends up as thermal energy spread through the surroundings, where it is no longer useful.
solution.answer_line: cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another

items.stem: A machine is supplied with 500 J and delivers 300 J of useful output. The 200 J that is left

misconception.label: Energy cannot be destroyed.

is still stored inside the machine

items.objective_statement: define pressure and apply definition
items.stem: Pressure in a liquid at a given depth acts

misconception.label: Pressure acts on the sides of a container as well as the base.
It acts on the base too, which is why the base has to be strong.
The upthrust on a submerged body is a consequence, not the whole of the pressure.

steps: The particles of a liquid move in all directions and collide with whatever they meet.
So the pressure at a point is the same whichever way a surface is turned.
It is this that makes hydraulic machines work.
solution.answer_line: equally in all directions

items.stem: A hydraulic jack can lift a heavy car with a small effort because

options.text: the liquid becomes lighter under pressure

misconception.label: The liquid's weight is unchanged and is not what matters.

options.text: the pressure applied to the small piston is transmitted undiminished to the larger piston
the liquid is compressed and stores energy

misconception.label: The liquid is very nearly incompressible, which is why it works.

options.text: the small piston moves the same distance as the large one

misconception.label: The small piston moves much further than the large one, which is the price paid for the larger force.

steps: Pressure applied at one point in a liquid is transmitted equally to every other point.
Force = pressure × area, so the same pressure on a larger piston gives a larger force.
Energy is not created: the small piston travels a long way to move the large one a little.

items.objective_statement: apply Archimedes’ principle to predict whether a body would float or sink in a given fluid
items.stem: A block of wood floats in water. This tells us that the density of the wood is

options.text: greater than the density of water

misconception.label: A body denser than water sinks.

options.text: equal to the density of water

misconception.label: A body of exactly the same density stays wherever it is put, fully submerged.

options.text: less than the density of water

misconception.label: Nothing has zero density.

steps: A floating body sinks until the weight of water it displaces equals its own weight.
It is only partly submerged, so it displaces a volume smaller than its own.
The same weight in a smaller volume means the water is denser, so the wood is the less dense of the two.
solution.answer_line: less than the density of water

items.objective_statement: relate the use of a thermometer to its design
items.stem: The bore of a thermometer is made very narrow in order to

misconception.label: A narrow bore holds less liquid, not more.

options.text: make a small change in volume produce a large movement of the column

misconception.label: A narrow bore does not slow the response; the bulb wall governs that.

options.text: widen the range of temperatures measured

misconception.label: A narrow bore actually shortens the range for a given tube length.

steps: The liquid in the bulb expands by a fixed volume for a given temperature rise.
That extra volume has to go somewhere, and it goes up the bore.
Length = volume ÷ cross sectional area, so a narrower bore gives a longer movement for the same expansion.
solution.answer_line: make a small change in volume produce a large movement of the column

misconception.label: Cost is not the design reason.

Thermal energy has to be conducted through the glass wall to get there.
A thin wall offers less resistance to that conduction, so the thermometer responds faster.

items.stem: Concrete roads are laid in sections with a gap between them because concrete

items.stem: A current carrying wire is placed at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The resultant field pattern is described as a catapult field because it

options.text: is strong on both sides of the wire

misconception.label: If both sides were equally strong there would be no sideways push.

options.text: is the same everywhere around the wire

misconception.label: An unequal pattern is the whole point; a symmetrical one would give no force.

options.text: is strong on one side of the wire and weak on the other

steps: Around the wire the field is a set of circles; the applied field is a set of parallel lines.
On one side the circles point the same way as the applied field, so the two add and the lines crowd.
On the other side they oppose and partly cancel, so the lines thin out.
The stretched lines act like a catapult and push the wire towards the weak side.
solution.answer_line: is strong on one side of the wire and weak on the other

items.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a galvanometer and then pulled out again. The galvanometer

options.text: deflects the same way both times

misconception.label: The two motions change the flux in opposite senses, so the deflections are opposite.
Pulling the magnet out changes the flux just as much as pushing it in.

options.text: deflects one way going in and the other way coming out

misconception.label: Both movements change the flux, so both induce a current.

steps: An e.m.f. is induced whenever the flux through the coil changes.
Pushing the magnet in increases the flux; pulling it out decreases it.
By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change, so it flows one way to oppose the increase and the other way to oppose the decrease.
solution.answer_line: deflects one way going in and the other way coming out

steps: As the coil turns, each side moves first one way across the field and then the other, so the induced e.m.f. reverses twice per revolution.

items.stem: In the step from P to Q, the proton number falls by 1 and the neutron number falls by 1. This step is

misconception.label: Beta decay turns a neutron into a proton, so the proton number rises while the neutron number falls.
Gamma emission changes neither number, so the point would not move at all.
The nuclide changes, so a decay has taken place.

steps: Alpha decay removes two protons and two neutrons, so both numbers fall together.
Beta decay converts a neutron into a proton, so Z rises by one while N falls by one: the point moves down and to the right.
Gamma emission changes neither Z nor N. P to Q moves down and to the left, with both falling, so it is the alpha step.
solution.answer_line: alpha decay

steps: In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted.
So the nucleus gains a proton and loses a neutron: Z rises by one and the mass number A is unchanged.

steps: Both processes release energy because the products have slightly less mass than the starting material.
